To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
serum thyroid hormone concentrations and thyroid gland weight in developing obese male Zucker rats are lower than in lean male Zucker rats.
serum thyroxine and thyrotrophins are lower in obese male Zucker rats than in lean littermates, and that serum 3,5-tri-iodothyronine is lower in obese than in control female rats.
The serum TSH levels in developing obese male rats were significantly lower than those in the lean littermates.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of thyroid hormones (TH) in the developing obese rat and their relation with the development of obesity.
the study of the development of thyroid function in the Zucker rat.
understanding the role of the hypothalamic-hypophyseo-thyroid axis in the development of the metabolic syndrome in the Zucker rat, a model of obesity and insulin resistance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
serum T4 is lower and serum TSH is higher in obese than in age-matched lean male rats.
the obese male Zucker rat is a hypothyroid animal.
the obese phenotype is associated with a decreased thyroid hormone secretion and that the obese phenotype in the Zucker rat is associated with decreased T3 and T4 secretion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
obese rats have lower serum T3 and T4 and lower serum TSH than lean rats.
the obese Zucker rats are a good model for the study of the development of obesity, and the development of thyroid dysfunction.
the development of obesity in Zucker rats is associated with a reduction in thyroid hormone levels.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are many factors that can affect the development of obesity in humans.
the thyroid is a target of obesity, and it is not just an organ that is involved in the regulation of metabolism.
the thyroid gland is not the only source of thyroid hormones in the body.
